screens.title: Wallet Management and Querying the Blockchain
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn the fundamentals of wallet management on Cardano and how to inspect what the chain knows about your addresses. We'll focus on generating cryptographic key pairs, building addresses that combine payment and stake credentials, and using cardano-cli to query UTxOs and protocol parameters. This matters because on Cardano a wallet is really a set of keys and addresses, not a single centralized account. That means you control funds with signing keys and expose public addresses derived from verification keys. As a concrete example, you'll generate payment and stake keys, build a base address for the preview testnet, fund it from a faucet, and then run a utxo query to see the unspent outputs. A common misconception is thinking a blockchain shows a single balance per address; on Cardano you must work with discrete UTxOs. By the end of this lesson you will understand the files produced by cardano-cli, how addresses differ by credential type, and why querying UTxOs matters when you later construct transactions. Keep security in mind: signing keys are the single sensitive secret that controls spending.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills You'll Build
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens we will develop four practical skills you can use immediately. First, you will generate payment and stake key pairs using cardano-cli and learn what each file contains. You will practice treating signing keys as secrets and verification keys as public identifiers. Second, you will construct different address types—base, enterprise, and stake—by combining verification keys appropriately, and you'll see how the presence or absence of a stake credential changes the address's capabilities. Third, you will run cardano-cli queries to inspect UTxOs and protocol parameters on the preview testnet, learning how to interpret TxHash, TxIx, amounts, and native tokens. Fourth, you will build familiarity with the EUTxO model so you can select inputs for transactions reliably. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify progress: generate keys, build a base. addr, fund it from a faucet, and successfully view its UTxOs. These skills are foundational for safe development and for composing transactions later in the course.

screens.title: Wallets are collections of keys, not single accounts
screens.narratorSegment: On Cardano a wallet is a conceptual grouping of key pairs rather than a single server-side account. Each key pair contains a signing key, which is private, and a verification key, which is public. The signing key authorizes spends: it proves to the network that the holder has the right to consume UTxOs controlled by the corresponding verification key. The verification key is used to derive addresses and can be safely shared when you want others to send funds to you. A good concrete example: when you run cardano-cli address key-gen for payment keys you create payment. skey and payment. vkey. The vkey is used to build the address; the skey must remain secret. A common misconception is to treat verification keys as secrets because they are used to build addresses; they are safe to publish. The real secret is the signing key. If you lose your signing key you lose control of funds; if someone else gains it they can spend your ADA. This screen also shows a simple analogy: think of the verification key as a mailbox address and the signing key as the private key to the mailbox. Keep signing keys offline and backed up, and never commit them to a repository. Why does this matter? Secure key handling prevents irreversible loss of funds and unauthorized spending, which is essential knowledge before you construct transactions.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Signing keys authorize spending and must be kept secret; verification keys derive addresses and can be shared.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Keys Overview
Definition
Signing key vs verification key
Signing key (.skey)
Private file used to authorize transactions. Must be kept secret and backed up.
Verification key (.vkey)
Public file used to derive addresses and verify signatures. Safe to share.
Analogy
Verification key is like a mailbox address where others send mail; signing key is the private mailbox key that opens and moves mail out.
Example files
payment.vkey, payment.skey, stake.vkey, stake.skey
Safety tip
Never store signing keys in public repos; use offline or encrypted backups.
Misconception
Verification keys are not secret even though they derive addresses.
Quick Example
cardano-cli address key-gen \
  --verification-key-file payment.vkey \
  --signing-key-file payment.skey
Key Takeaway

Treat .skey as the single sensitive secret for spending; .vkey lets others send funds by deriving addresses.

screens.title: Payment keys vs Stake keys
screens.narratorSegment: Cardano separates payment and stake responsibilities into different key pairs. Payment keys control spending: when you build a transaction you sign inputs with the payment signing key to consume UTxOs. Stake keys are for delegation and registering stake addresses; they are not used to authorize spending. A base address combines a payment verification key and a stake verification key, enabling both spending and stake delegation. An enterprise address contains only a payment credential and cannot be used for staking. This separation is useful: for example, an exchange might use enterprise addresses for deposits where staking is not required, while a delegated personal wallet uses base addresses to earn rewards. A common error is creating an address without the intended credential and assuming staking will work; always confirm the address type you built. The practical consequence shows up when you register a stake key and delegate: stake rewards are associated with the stake credential present in the base address. Remember: keep signing keys secure, and choose address types based on whether you need stake delegation. Payment keys vs Stake keys means payment keys enable spends; stake keys enable delegation. base addresses combine both; enterprise addresses have only payment credentials.. In practical terms, roles, uses, and how they combine in addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Compare
keyIdea.text: Payment keys enable spends; stake keys enable delegation. Base addresses combine both; enterprise addresses have only payment credentials.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Payment vs Stake
Payment Keys
Used to sign transactions and consume UTxOs. Files: payment.skey and payment.vkey.
Enterprise Address
Built with a payment verification key only; cannot delegate stake.
Stake Keys
Used for delegation and registering stake addresses. Files: stake.skey and stake.vkey.
When to use each: enterprise addresses for one-off payments or custodial deposit flows; base addresses when you plan to delegate.
Base Address
Combine payment.vkey and stake.vkey to produce a base.addr. This address supports both spending and staking activities.
Example
cardano-cli address build \
  --payment-verification-key-file payment.vkey \
  --stake-verification-key-file stake.vkey \
  --out-file base.addr \
  --testnet-magic 2
Common mistake

Building an enterprise.addr when you intended to delegate stake will prevent delegation and reward accrual.

screens.title: Generate keys with cardano-cli
screens.narratorSegment: Generating keys is the first hands-on step and uses straightforward cardano-cli commands. When you run the payment key generation command you create a payment. vkey and payment. skey file. Similarly, the stake key generation produces stake. vkey and stake. skey. These files are ordinary text files in JSON or key-encoded format that cardano-cli reads later when building addresses or signing transactions. A concrete step-by-step: create a directory for keys, then run cardano-cli address key-gen for payment keys and cardano-cli stake-address key-gen for stake keys. After generation, confirm files exist and inspect their contents in a safe environment — do not paste signing key contents into a public terminal. A common misconception is that generating keys is risky; the real risk is mishandling the signing key afterward. Example commands are displayed in the code panel so you can copy them into a terminal. As you practice, treat the verification keys as public and signing keys as secret. At the end of this step, you will have four files that serve as inputs to address generation and future transaction signing. Generate keys with cardano-cli means use cardano-cli address key-gen and stake-address key-gen to create payment and stake key pairs; inspect and secure the signing keys.. In practical terms, terminal-first commands and file outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Generate keys
keyIdea.text: Use cardano-cli address key-gen and stake-address key-gen to create payment and stake key pairs; inspect and secure the signing keys.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Key Generation
Terminal Commands
Run these steps to create key files used later for addresses and signing.
mkdir wallet-keys
cd wallet-keys

cardano-cli address key-gen \
  --verification-key-file payment.vkey \
  --signing-key-file payment.skey

cardano-cli stake-address key-gen \
  --verification-key-file stake.vkey \
  --signing-key-file stake.skey
Inspect files safely with a local text editor. Never publish .skey contents.
File roles
payment.vkey — public verification key used in address construction. payment.skey — private signing key used for transaction authorization.
Safety checklist
  • Back up signing keys securely.
  • Do not commit signing keys to version control.
  • Use verification keys when sharing an address publicly.
Key Takeaway

Generate four files: payment.vkey, payment.skey, stake.vkey, stake.skey. Protect the .skey files as the secret that controls funds.

screens.title: Build a base and enterprise address
screens.narratorSegment: Building an address ties verification keys to a public identifier where funds will arrive. To create a base address you supply both the payment verification key and stake verification key to cardano-cli address build. The presence of the stake verification key embeds a stake credential, enabling delegation. To create an enterprise address, omit the stake verification key and the resulting address will only contain a payment credential. A clear example: the command cardano-cli address build with --payment-verification-key-file payment. vkey --stake-verification-key-file stake. vkey produces base. addr. If you run the same command without the stake option and direct output to enterprise. addr, you've made an enterprise address. Use the appropriate --testnet-magic for your network; for preview testnet use magic 2. After building the address, cat the. addr file to display the human-readable address string that you will copy to a faucet. A common pitfall is using the wrong testnet magic or forgetting to cat the file to copy the address, which leads to funding the wrong chain. Confirm the file contents before requesting test ADA. Build a base and enterprise address means base addresses include both payment and stake verification keys; enterprise addresses include payment only. use testnet magic for the correct network.. In practical terms, command patterns and the role of --stake-verification-key-file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Address construction
keyIdea.text: Base addresses include both payment and stake verification keys; enterprise addresses include payment only. Use testnet magic for the correct network.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Address Building
Build Commands
Create a base address by supplying both verification keys. Omit stake to build an enterprise address.
cardano-cli address build \
  --payment-verification-key-file payment.vkey \
  --stake-verification-key-file stake.vkey \
  --out-file base.addr \
  --testnet-magic 2

# Enterprise address (no stake key)
cardano-cli address build \
  --payment-verification-key-file payment.vkey \
  --out-file enterprise.addr \
  --testnet-magic 2

cat base.addr
After building, cat the .addr file to copy the string you will use at a faucet. Verify the testnet magic matches the network you intend.
Example
base.addr contains the address; copy it to request test ADA from a preview faucet.
Pitfall
Using the wrong testnet magic or funding an enterprise address when you expected staking will cause confusion; double-check before funding.
Key Takeaway

Choose base or enterprise based on whether you want stake delegation. Always verify the address string before requesting funds.

screens.title: EUTxO model explained
screens.narratorSegment: Cardano uses an Extended Unspent Transaction Output model, or EUTxO, to represent funds. Rather than a single account balance, your funds are a collection of discrete UTxOs. Each UTxO is tied to an address, contains a specific amount of ADA and possibly native tokens, and references the transaction that created it. When you spend funds you consume one or more UTxOs as inputs and produce new UTxOs as outputs. This model makes parallelism and deterministic script validation easier, but it requires you to explicitly select which UTxOs to spend when building transactions. A concrete example: if your address has two UTxOs of 1 ADA and 5 ADA and you need to send 2 ADA, you would typically select the 5 ADA UTxO as an input and produce change back to yourself. A common misunderstanding is to think all ADA at an address is a single balance; with EUTxO you must work with discrete outputs. Understanding this is essential before constructing transactions because fees, minimum UTxO values, and token bundles affect how you select and combine inputs and outputs. EUTxO model explained means funds are discrete outputs that must be selected and consumed; transactions consume inputs and create new outputs.. In practical terms, why cardano represents funds as unspent outputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: EUTxO concept
keyIdea.text: Funds are discrete outputs that must be selected and consumed; transactions consume inputs and create new outputs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › EUTxO
What is a UTxO?
An unspent transaction output tied to a specific address, amount, and optional tokens. Each line in a utxo query represents one spendable output.
Example scenario
Address has UTxOs: 1 ADA and 5 ADA. To send 2 ADA, use the 5 ADA UTxO as input and create a change output back to the original address.
Why it matters
Input selection determines which tokens and how much ADA are consumed, and it interacts with fees and minimum UTxO values when building transactions.
Misconception

Treating the address as a single balance will lead to incorrect input selection and failed transactions.

UTxO Analogy
Think of UTxOs as coins in your wallet of fixed denominations; you choose which coins to use to pay an amount and get change back.
Key Takeaway

Plan input selection and be aware of minimum UTxO constraints when combining outputs and tokens.

screens.title: Query UTxOs with cardano-cli
screens.narratorSegment: To inspect the unspent outputs at an address use cardano-cli query utxo. Before running the command ensure CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH points to your synced node's socket and that you specify the correct testnet magic. The command returns a table with TxHash, TxIx, and Amount columns; each line is a spendable output. A concrete command sequence sets the socket path, then runs cardano-cli query utxo --address $(cat base. addr) --testnet-magic 2. The output shows a transaction hash and index pair identifying the originating output, and the amount in lovelace plus any native tokens listed. For example, a line with 1,000,000 lovelace represents 1 ADA. Use these TxHash and TxIx values when selecting inputs for new transactions. A common mistake is running the query before the node is fully synced or using the wrong socket path, leading to empty results. Also remember that an empty utxo list means no funds at that address. After the query, you will know which outputs you can consume when constructing a transaction. Query UTxOs with cardano-cli means use cardano-cli query utxo with correct cardano_node_socket_path and testnet magic to list spendable outputs by txhash and txix.. In practical terms, commands, required environment variables, and reading output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Query UTxOs
Ensure node socket is set
Set CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH to your node socket before running queries.

Read the output table carefully: each row corresponds to a TxHash and TxIx pair and lists amounts including lovelace and native tokens. These rows are the inputs you can reference when building transactions.
Interpreting output
TxHash and TxIx uniquely identify an output. Amount shows ADA in lovelace and any attached tokens.
Common mistake
Running the query before node sync or with the wrong socket will show no UTxOs. Verify the node is fully synced.

screens.title: Interpreting a UTxO table
screens.narratorSegment: When you run a utxo query the table lists each unspent output with a TxHash, TxIx, and Amount. The TxHash and TxIx together pinpoint the exact output you will reference when building a transaction. The Amount column shows lovelace and any native token bundles. For instance, a line showing 1,000,000 lovelace + 10 NFT. TokenName means that output includes 1 ADA and an attached token bundle. To send 2 ADA you must select inputs whose combined lovelace covers the amount plus fees and any required minimum UTxO values. In our example with a 1 ADA and a 5 ADA UTxO, the 5 ADA output is sufficient and will produce change back to your address. A common mistake is forgetting minimum UTxO or token bundle constraints which can invalidate outputs. Also, consuming an output with an attached token moves that token unless you explicitly return it in a change output. When selecting inputs, list the TxHash#TxIx pairs in your transaction builder and ensure the sum minus fees equals desired outputs plus change. This explicit selection process is central to correctly constructing Cardano transactions.

screens.title: Pitfalls and security practices
screens.narratorSegment: As you practice, watch for a few recurring mistakes. First, forgetting to set CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH or using an unsynced node often produces empty utxo results; always confirm node sync. Second, using the wrong testnet magic sends queries to a different network and gives misleading outputs—match your faucet and build commands to the same network magic. Third, mishandling signing keys by committing them to repositories or storing them in shared folders can lead to irreversible loss if an attacker obtains them. Fourth, misinterpreting utxo output by treating it as a single balance causes incorrect input selection; remember UTxOs are discrete. Finally, when dealing with token bundles, remember that consuming an input with tokens transfers ownership of those tokens unless you include them in change outputs. Practical checks: verify file contents, double-check address strings before funding, and refresh protocol parameters before building transactions. Reflect on these checks before creating any transaction to reduce the risk of loss or failed submissions. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn the fundamentals of wallet management on Cardano and how to inspect what the chain knows about your addresses. We'll focus on generating cryptographic key pairs, building addresses that combine payment and stake credentials, and using cardano-cli to query UTxOs and protocol parameters. This matters because on Cardano a wallet is really a set of keys and addresses, not a single centralized account. That means you control funds with signing keys and expose public addresses derived from verification keys. As a concrete example, you'll generate payment and stake keys, build a base address for the preview testnet, fund it from a faucet, and then run a utxo query to see the unspent outputs. A common misconception is thinking a blockchain shows a single balance per address; on Cardano you must work with discrete UTxOs. By the end of this lesson you will understand the files produced by cardano-cli, how addresses differ by credential type, and why querying UTxOs matters when you later construct transactions. Keep security in mind: signing keys are the single sensitive secret that controls spending.

Over the next screens we will develop four practical skills you can use immediately. First, you will generate payment and stake key pairs using cardano-cli and learn what each file contains. You will practice treating signing keys as secrets and verification keys as public identifiers. Second, you will construct different address types—base, enterprise, and stake—by combining verification keys appropriately, and you'll see how the presence or absence of a stake credential changes the address's capabilities. Third, you will run cardano-cli queries to inspect UTxOs and protocol parameters on the preview testnet, learning how to interpret TxHash, TxIx, amounts, and native tokens. Fourth, you will build familiarity with the EUTxO model so you can select inputs for transactions reliably. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify progress: generate keys, build a base. addr, fund it from a faucet, and successfully view its UTxOs. These skills are foundational for safe development and for composing transactions later in the course.

We will use a simple Bloom progression to frame practice. First, Learn: generate the files and confirm their presence on disk. Understand: explain the difference between signing and verification keys and why each matters. Apply: build a base address and query it after funding with a faucet, interpreting the utxo table to pick inputs. Master: compose a real transaction later that selects UTxOs and respects protocol parameters. A practical verification path is provided for each step: create payment. vkey and payment. skey, then stake. vkey and stake. skey, then build base. addr and run cardano-cli query utxo to see outputs. Remember to set CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH and to use the correct testnet magic for preview. The progression helps you move from file-level tasks to reasoning about how discrete UTxOs are consumed during spends and why protocol parameters influence fee calculation. Keep these milestones visible as you follow hands-on activities.

On Cardano a wallet is a conceptual grouping of key pairs rather than a single server-side account. Each key pair contains a signing key, which is private, and a verification key, which is public. The signing key authorizes spends: it proves to the network that the holder has the right to consume UTxOs controlled by the corresponding verification key. The verification key is used to derive addresses and can be safely shared when you want others to send funds to you. A good concrete example: when you run cardano-cli address key-gen for payment keys you create payment. skey and payment. vkey. The vkey is used to build the address; the skey must remain secret. A common misconception is to treat verification keys as secrets because they are used to build addresses; they are safe to publish. The real secret is the signing key. If you lose your signing key you lose control of funds; if someone else gains it they can spend your ADA. This screen also shows a simple analogy: think of the verification key as a mailbox address and the signing key as the private key to the mailbox. Keep signing keys offline and backed up, and never commit them to a repository. Why does this matter? Secure key handling prevents irreversible loss of funds and unauthorized spending, which is essential knowledge before you construct transactions.

Cardano separates payment and stake responsibilities into different key pairs. Payment keys control spending: when you build a transaction you sign inputs with the payment signing key to consume UTxOs. Stake keys are for delegation and registering stake addresses; they are not used to authorize spending. A base address combines a payment verification key and a stake verification key, enabling both spending and stake delegation. An enterprise address contains only a payment credential and cannot be used for staking. This separation is useful: for example, an exchange might use enterprise addresses for deposits where staking is not required, while a delegated personal wallet uses base addresses to earn rewards. A common error is creating an address without the intended credential and assuming staking will work; always confirm the address type you built. The practical consequence shows up when you register a stake key and delegate: stake rewards are associated with the stake credential present in the base address. Remember: keep signing keys secure, and choose address types based on whether you need stake delegation. Payment keys vs Stake keys means payment keys enable spends; stake keys enable delegation. base addresses combine both; enterprise addresses have only payment credentials.. In practical terms, roles, uses, and how they combine in addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Generating keys is the first hands-on step and uses straightforward cardano-cli commands. When you run the payment key generation command you create a payment. vkey and payment. skey file. Similarly, the stake key generation produces stake. vkey and stake. skey. These files are ordinary text files in JSON or key-encoded format that cardano-cli reads later when building addresses or signing transactions. A concrete step-by-step: create a directory for keys, then run cardano-cli address key-gen for payment keys and cardano-cli stake-address key-gen for stake keys. After generation, confirm files exist and inspect their contents in a safe environment — do not paste signing key contents into a public terminal. A common misconception is that generating keys is risky; the real risk is mishandling the signing key afterward. Example commands are displayed in the code panel so you can copy them into a terminal. As you practice, treat the verification keys as public and signing keys as secret. At the end of this step, you will have four files that serve as inputs to address generation and future transaction signing. Generate keys with cardano-cli means use cardano-cli address key-gen and stake-address key-gen to create payment and stake key pairs; inspect and secure the signing keys.. In practical terms, terminal-first commands and file outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Building an address ties verification keys to a public identifier where funds will arrive. To create a base address you supply both the payment verification key and stake verification key to cardano-cli address build. The presence of the stake verification key embeds a stake credential, enabling delegation. To create an enterprise address, omit the stake verification key and the resulting address will only contain a payment credential. A clear example: the command cardano-cli address build with --payment-verification-key-file payment. vkey --stake-verification-key-file stake. vkey produces base. addr. If you run the same command without the stake option and direct output to enterprise. addr, you've made an enterprise address. Use the appropriate --testnet-magic for your network; for preview testnet use magic 2. After building the address, cat the. addr file to display the human-readable address string that you will copy to a faucet. A common pitfall is using the wrong testnet magic or forgetting to cat the file to copy the address, which leads to funding the wrong chain. Confirm the file contents before requesting test ADA. Build a base and enterprise address means base addresses include both payment and stake verification keys; enterprise addresses include payment only. use testnet magic for the correct network.. In practical terms, command patterns and the role of --stake-verification-key-file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cardano uses an Extended Unspent Transaction Output model, or EUTxO, to represent funds. Rather than a single account balance, your funds are a collection of discrete UTxOs. Each UTxO is tied to an address, contains a specific amount of ADA and possibly native tokens, and references the transaction that created it. When you spend funds you consume one or more UTxOs as inputs and produce new UTxOs as outputs. This model makes parallelism and deterministic script validation easier, but it requires you to explicitly select which UTxOs to spend when building transactions. A concrete example: if your address has two UTxOs of 1 ADA and 5 ADA and you need to send 2 ADA, you would typically select the 5 ADA UTxO as an input and produce change back to yourself. A common misunderstanding is to think all ADA at an address is a single balance; with EUTxO you must work with discrete outputs. Understanding this is essential before constructing transactions because fees, minimum UTxO values, and token bundles affect how you select and combine inputs and outputs. EUTxO model explained means funds are discrete outputs that must be selected and consumed; transactions consume inputs and create new outputs.. In practical terms, why cardano represents funds as unspent outputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Here are three compact concepts to carry forward. First: Payment and stake keys are distinct. Payment keys control spending; stake keys control delegation and are combined in base addresses when you want both capabilities. Second: Addresses are derived from verification keys. A base address includes both payment and stake credentials; an enterprise address includes only a payment credential and cannot be used for staking. Third: Cardano uses the EUTxO model. Funds are represented as discrete unspent outputs; you must query and select specific UTxOs by TxHash and TxIx when building transactions. Keep these three ideas in mind as they govern how you manage wallets, construct addresses, and craft transactions on Cardano.
